passage: Afreen's talk on warehouse costs last week had forty-one slides, and I counted. I'm Samir, and I promise I was trying. Afreen started with six charts on one slide, then a table, then sub-tables, and by slide twelve I was checking messages. Afterwards a colleague asked me what the point was. I said, "Costs... something about pallets?" Ask what I remember and it is that Afreen is clearly smart and the talk felt long. Ask for the message and I've got nothing. The one thing I could repeat was the very last slide, where she said, "We can cut one delivery a week." If she had opened with that, I would have listened to the rest.

qa.q: How many slides did Afreen's talk have?
qa.a: It had forty-one slides.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling by slide twelve?
qa.a: Losing interest and drifting, checking messages instead of following.

qa.q: What could Afreen have done differently?
qa.a: Open with the main message that one delivery a week can be cut, and keep only the slides that support it.

qa.q: How might Afreen have seen the talk?
qa.a: Afreen probably felt that sharing every detail showed thoroughness, without realising the audience had lost the point.

grounding: Shows a listener who stops following a talk full of details with no clear message and recalls only one line.

passage: I'm Hemant, a resident of Block C, and I sat at the back of the society's general meeting. Avni, the new secretary, showed twenty-three slides of accounts: line after line of small amounts. Halfway through, the man beside me was counting ceiling tiles, and a woman in front had started a shopping list on her phone. I lost track after the lift repair figures. When Avni said, "So, in summary, we need to decide about the water tank," half the room was already reaching for bags. I don't know how nervous Avni was. I do know I left remembering only that the tank was mentioned, not what decision was needed.

qa.q: How many slides of accounts did Avni show?
qa.a: Avni showed twenty-three slides of accounts.

qa.q: What might Hemant be feeling about leaving without knowing the decision?
qa.a: Frustrated and let down, because after the whole talk the decision was not clear.

qa.q: What could Avni change so people remember the decision?
qa.a: Start with the water tank decision, keep a few key figures and put the detailed accounts in a handout.

qa.q: What might Avni be experiencing as the room reaches for bags?
qa.a: Possibly discouragement or worry, though Hemant admits not knowing how nervous Avni was.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing an audience drift away from a presenter who piles on details with no clear message.

passage:
Week one. Chinmay sat in the Monday review as Tushar went through forty slides of sales data. Tables, then more tables. By slide twelve Chinmay realised he had stopped reading and was thinking about lunch. He felt a bit guilty and tried to focus again. He couldn't find the thread.
Week two. Same meeting, thirty-five slides. Chinmay noticed the manager scrolling on her phone. When Tushar asked, "Any questions?", nobody had one. Chinmay wanted to ask what the main point was, but it felt rude.
Week three. On Wednesday, the manager stopped Chinmay in the corridor. "What did Tushar's review say about the south region?" Chinmay tried. He remembered one chart, a red line going down in March, and Tushar saying, "That's the store that closed." That was all. Forty slides, and one sentence stayed.
That afternoon Chinmay messaged Tushar: "Can I show you something about your deck?"

qa.q: How many slides did Tushar show in week one?
qa.a: Tushar went through forty slides of sales data.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling in week two when nobody had a question?
qa.a: Chinmay felt uneasy and hesitant, wanting to ask for the main point but worried it would seem rude.

qa.q: What could Chinmay show Tushar that might help his next deck?
qa.a: That the one clear chart with a simple sentence was the only part remembered, so a few clear points would work better than forty slides.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel if he learned what people remembered?
qa.a: Tushar might feel surprised and a little hurt that all the detail was lost, but it could help him see what actually lands.

grounding: An observer across three weeks sees a presenter bury the message in detail and finds that only one clear point was remembered.

passage:
Vidya, you're giving your first big talk next week? Sit. Your Rajni aunty has a story.
When I was a young officer, maybe twenty-four, I was sent to a state conference on rural water. The main speaker was a senior engineer, very respected. He had brought sixty slides. Tables of pipe lengths, rainfall for every district, costs by year. He read them very fast.
I had a notebook. I tried to write. By the twentieth slide I had written only the date. The man next to me was asleep. I felt terrible for the engineer, and also, honestly, annoyed. I had taken a night bus to be there.
You know what I remember from that whole hour? One photograph. A girl carrying two pots on her head, and his one sentence: "She walks four kilometres. This project cuts it to two hundred metres."
Forty years later, I remember that girl. I don't remember a single table.

qa.q: What was the one photograph Rajni remembers?
qa.a: A girl carrying two pots on her head.

qa.q: How did young Rajni feel as the slides went on?
qa.a: Rajni felt sorry for the engineer and also annoyed, having taken a night bus to be there.

qa.q: At what point in the talk did the engineer finally reach his audience?
qa.a: When he showed the photograph and said one clear sentence about the walk being cut to two hundred metres.

qa.q: How might the engineer have seen his own talk?
qa.a: The engineer probably thought all the tables showed how thorough the project was, not noticing that people had stopped following.

grounding: An elder recalls a talk full of detail with no clear message, where only one clear image and sentence were remembered.

passage:
The community hall in Hamilton was hot; the ceiling fans had broken the week before. Thomas had come straight from his shift to hear the council's plan for the flooded streets on his side of town.
Sonali, the council's planning officer, opened a laptop. Slide after slide: rainfall charts from 1998, pipe diameters, three alternative budgets, a map too small to read from the back. She spoke quickly, reading numbers aloud.
Thomas tried. He really did. His street flooded twice last winter. But after ten minutes he was fanning himself with the leaflet, and after twenty he was checking the time. Around him, people whispered to each other: "Are they fixing it or not?"
At the very end, Sonali said, "So, the Fourth Street drain gets replaced in spring." Thomas sat up. That was it. That was the thing he'd come for, in the last ten seconds.
Walking out, he heard three different people repeat that one line.

qa.q: Why was the community hall hot?
qa.a: The ceiling fans had broken the week before.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel as the slides went on?
qa.a: Thomas felt frustrated and restless, fanning himself and checking the time while trying to find the point.

qa.q: What could Sonali have done differently at the start?
qa.a: Sonali could have opened with the one clear message, that the Fourth Street drain gets replaced in spring, and kept the detail for questions.

qa.q: How might Sonali see the evening?
qa.a: Sonali may think she gave a thorough report, without realising most people only heard the last line.

grounding: Shows a listener who stops following a detail-heavy talk and remembers only the one clear point given at the end.

passage: At the NGO's quarterly volunteer meeting in a Chennai school hall, Ankita sat in the fourth row with a notebook, determined to follow Payal's report on the reading programme. Slide one: enrolment by ward. Slide two: enrolment by age. Slide three: attendance by month, by ward, by age. Payal talked fast, pointing at columns. By slide nine Ankita had stopped writing. By slide fifteen she was wondering whether the canteen had idlis left, and felt guilty about it. Around her, two volunteers were scrolling their phones and the man beside her was drawing boxes in the margin. Then, near the end, almost as an aside, Payal said, "Oh, and Arif, eight, read the number on his bus by himself last week." The whole room looked up. Walking out, Ankita tried to recall a single figure from the thirty slides and couldn't. But that night she told her flatmate about Arif and the bus.

qa.q: What did Arif do by himself last week?
qa.a: He read the number on his bus.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel by slide fifteen?
qa.a: Ankita was bored and a little guilty for drifting off to thoughts of idlis, despite meaning to follow closely.

qa.q: What could Payal change in the next report?
qa.a: Lead with one clear message and a story like Arif's, then show just a few key figures that support it, instead of thirty slides of columns.

qa.q: What might Payal have hoped the thirty slides would show?
qa.a: Payal probably wanted to prove how much work and progress the programme had made, and may not have realised the room stopped following.

grounding: Shows a listener who stops following a report full of detail with no clear message, and remembers only the one story that made sense.
